The other day, I found an old journal tucked between the pages of a book in my parents’ attic. The paper was yellowed, the ink faded, but the words still held a strange, electric charge. It was my grandmother’s handwriting—loops and swirls that looked like they were dancing across the page. The last entry was dated 1987, just a few years before she passed. She’d written about the first time she saw the ocean, not from a beach in some postcard-perfect place, but from the deck of a rusty ferry, the salt air stinging her eyes as she clutched her mother’s hand. *"It was bigger than anything I’d ever imagined,"* she’d scribbled, *"and for a moment, I forgot how to breathe."*

I’ve always loved the ocean, but reading that made it feel like something more than just waves and tides. It was a place of awe, of quiet revelation. My grandmother never traveled much after that—she spent her life in a small town, raising kids, working in a library—but she carried that memory with her, like a secret. I wonder if she ever went back, if she stood on a shore and let the water whisper to her again.

Now, when I’m near the coast, I think of her. The way the light hits the water at dusk, how the gulls scream like they’re arguing with the sky. Maybe that’s what memories are—tiny, glowing embers of moments we’ve lived, waiting to be rekindled by the right wind.

I don’t know why I’m telling you this. Maybe because sometimes, the things that matter most aren’t the grand gestures or the big stories, but the quiet ones—the ones that make you pause and realize the world is still full of magic, if you know where to look.
